action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral putaminal atrophy with a T2/FLAIR rim and SWI hypointensity, pontine hot cross bun sign with pontine atrophy, and middle cerebellar peduncle and cerebellar atrophy (MDS 2022 MRI markers); Fazekas grade 2 white matter change and an old 5 mm left cerebellar lacune; normal midbrain
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude a structural, vascular or atypical-parkinsonism cause
action_criteria.rationale: PD is a clinical diagnosis; MRI is normal in PD and excludes vascular lesions, NPH, mass and the midbrain, pontine and putaminal signs of PSP and MSA [Postuma_2015]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal cardiac MIBG uptake: early H/M 2.40, delayed H/M 2.20, washout 20%
action_criteria.label: Consider cardiac MIBG scintigraphy
action_criteria.rationale: Cardiac sympathetic innervation is usually preserved in MSA and reduced in PD and DLB; with the MRI markers already present the result is supportive only [Wenning_2022]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: REM sleep without atonia in 58% of REM epochs with two dream-enactment episodes; recurrent inspiratory stridor in NREM and REM sleep; AHI 12.4/h with SpO2 nadir 86%
action_criteria.label: Consider video-polysomnography for the dream enactment and the nocturnal breathing noise
action_criteria.rationale: His wife reports dream enactment and a new high-pitched inspiratory noise in sleep; video-PSG confirms REM sleep without atonia and documents nocturnal stridor and sleep apnoea, which change the airway management [Wenning_2022]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Impaired processing speed (PSI 74), working memory (WMI 84), Trail Making B (132 s), Stroop interference (z -2.0) and FAS fluency (24 words), with preserved comprehension, reasoning, naming and figure copy
action_criteria.label: Consider a neuropsychological battery
action_criteria.rationale: MoCA 24/30 with errors on trail-making, fluency and recall; the battery characterises the deficit and confirms that it falls short of dementia, which within 3 years of motor onset would argue against MSA [Wenning_2022]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amlodipine, tamsulosin and propranolol identified as adding to the orthostatic fall with levodopa; supine pressure monitoring noted for midodrine
action_criteria.label: Review the medication list for drugs that worsen orthostatic hypotension
action_criteria.rationale: Amlodipine 10 mg, tamsulosin and propranolol each add to a 44/28 mmHg orthostatic fall that already causes near-syncope, and any pressor treatment must take the supine hypertension into account [Wenning_2022]

prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, haloperidol or other centrally acting D2-blocking antiemetics or antipsychotics; if an antipsychotic is needed, use quetiapine or clozapine
Do not add drugs that worsen orthostatic hypotension (diuretics, further alpha-blockers or vasodilators)
Do not start an antimuscarinic for the urge incontinence before the post-void residual is known: it worsens incomplete emptying and adds to the cognitive impairment
Do not give clonazepam or another sedative hypnotic for the dream enactment before the stridor has been assessed
required_recommendations: Diagnose clinically established MSA (MDS 2022), predominantly parkinsonian with cerebellar features: autonomic dysfunction (neurogenic orthostatic hypotension 44/28 mmHg at 3 minutes, urge incontinence), poorly levodopa-responsive parkinsonism (600 mg/day for 6 weeks with at most 10-15% subjective benefit) and a cerebellar syndrome (gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria), supportive features of moderate postural instability within 3 years, anterocollis and nocturnal inspiratory stridor, and MRI markers (putaminal atrophy with SWI signal decrease, pontine and middle cerebellar peduncle atrophy, hot cross bun sign) [Wenning_2022]

Arrange urgent ENT laryngoscopy for the nocturnal inspiratory stridor (vocal cord abductor weakness carries a risk of sudden death in sleep), with CPAP or tracheostomy according to the findings [Wenning_2022]

Treat the neurogenic orthostatic hypotension: taper propranolol (prescribed for the old tremor, which no longer needs it) after confirming with cardiology that it has no coronary indication; review tamsulosin and stop daytime amlodipine, treating any supine hypertension with head-up tilt of the bed and, if needed, a short-acting agent at bedtime; non-pharmacological measures (fluids and salt, compression garments, slow rising, smaller meals); and consider midodrine or droxidopa if symptoms persist, monitoring the supine pressure (148/90 mmHg before treatment)
Measure the post-void residual and assess the bladder before any prostate treatment; intermittent catheterisation if the residual is 100 mL or more

Complete the levodopa trial toward 1000 mg/day as tolerated over at least a month, with lying and standing blood pressure at each step, and taper it slowly rather than stopping abruptly if there is still no benefit

Arrange physiotherapy and fall prevention, speech and swallowing assessment for the dysarthria, bedroom safety for the dream enactment (melatonin rather than clonazepam until the stridor and any sleep apnoea have been assessed and treated), and multidisciplinary follow-up including a discussion of prognosis and palliative-care support

avoided_actions.rationale: No seizure, transient loss of awareness without a postural trigger or encephalopathy: EEG does not inform this parkinsonism
No inflammatory, infectious or rapidly progressive cognitive feature: CSF has no role in the MSA work-up
No murmur, heart failure or exertional symptom: the near-syncope occurs on standing with a documented orthostatic fall, and the echocardiogram does not inform it
A DaTscan does not separate PD from MSA or PSP [Marshall_2009]
Formal autonomic testing is not needed: bedside orthostatic blood pressure already documents the neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Formal autonomic testing is not needed: bedside orthostatic blood pressure already documents the neurogenic orthostatic hypotension

accepted: Multiple system atrophy with mixed parkinsonian and cerebellar features (MSA-P/C overlap)

differential.key_features: Cerebellar ataxia is an MDS 2015 absolute exclusion, and symmetric parkinsonism without rest tremor, early falls and severe autonomic failure are red flags; no benefit from 600 mg/day levodopa; MSA MRI markers. The single 5 mm left cerebellar lacune does not explain bilateral ataxia
The old bilateral action tremor with a family history in father and brother may have been essential tremor and may coexist; it does not explain the parkinsonism, ataxia or autonomic failure

Vascular risk factors, Fazekas grade 2 and an old cerebellar lacune, but upper-limb bradykinesia and rigidity, no basal ganglia infarcts, symmetric ataxia, autonomic failure and MSA markers: coexisting small-vessel disease, not the cause

differential.diagnosis: Drug contribution to the orthostatic hypotension (amlodipine, tamsulosin, propranolol)
differential.key_features: Coexists and adds to the fall, but the fall persisted when amlodipine was halved and comes with urge incontinence, constipation and stridor: autonomic failure, not a drug effect alone
Sporadic onset at 73 with no family history of ataxia; severe autonomic failure and parkinsonism
No vertical gaze palsy and normal-speed vertical saccades; normal midbrain area without hummingbird sign; severe dysautonomia and ataxia are not PSP features
No dementia (MMSE 27/30, MoCA 24/30), no fluctuations or visual hallucinations; RBD and orthostatic hypotension occur in DLB, but ataxia and pontocerebellar MRI markers do not

key_clinical_evidence: Symmetric bradykinesia with decrement and lead-pipe rigidity, no rest tremor; no benefit from levodopa 600 mg/day for 6 weeks (at most 10-15% subjective improvement)

Cerebellar syndrome: bilateral heel-to-shin ataxia, wide-based gait with failed tandem walking, saccadic pursuit and slurred, irregular speech; a single 5 mm left cerebellar lacune does not explain it

Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension: 148/90 mmHg supine to 104/62 mmHg at 3 minutes (44/28 mmHg), persisting after amlodipine was halved; the heart-rate rise of 8/min is blunted also by propranolol [Wenning_2022]
Urge incontinence, worsening constipation, dream enactment and a new inspiratory noise in sleep (stridor)
Moderate postural instability with falls within the first 16 months, and mild anterocollis
MRI: putaminal atrophy with a T2/FLAIR rim and SWI hypointensity, hot cross bun sign, pontine and middle cerebellar peduncle atrophy (MDS 2022 MRI markers) [Wenning_2022]
Cerebellar ataxia is an MDS 2015 absolute exclusion for PD [Postuma_2015]

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Antihypertensives, tamsulosin and propranolol add to the fall, but a 44/28 mmHg fall that persisted after the amlodipine dose was halved, with bladder and bowel dysfunction, is neurogenic

red_herrings.data_point: Old 5 mm left cerebellar lacunar infarct and Fazekas grade 2 small-vessel change

interactions: Tamsulosin (alpha-1 blocker) lowers standing blood pressure and adds to the orthostatic fall; levodopa can lower it further. Review the need for each and measure lying and standing blood pressure at each levodopa dose step.
Amlodipine 10 mg lowers standing blood pressure and adds to the orthostatic fall; levodopa can lower it further.
Propranolol lowers standing blood pressure and blunts the compensatory heart-rate rise on standing; with levodopa the orthostatic fall can deepen.
Aspirin, atorvastatin and polyethylene glycol 3350: no interaction with levodopa.
warnings: Midodrine, if used for orthostatic hypotension, raises supine blood pressure (supine 148/90 mmHg before treatment): measure the supine pressure before and during treatment and give the last dose at least 4 hours before lying down. Tamsulosin opposes the alpha-1 agonist effect of midodrine.
Fludrocortisone causes supine hypertension, fluid retention and hypokalaemia.
Benzodiazepines such as clonazepam add sedation and fall risk with dopaminergic drugs in older patients and can depress breathing during sleep.
Antimuscarinic bladder drugs worsen incomplete bladder emptying and add to constipation and confusion.
Penicillin allergy recorded: not relevant to the dopaminergic options.

additional_observations: No acute infarcts on DWI sequences
No ventriculomegaly out of proportion to sulcal atrophy
Middle cerebellar peduncles appear atrophic with subtle T2 signal change

metadata.condition_name: Parkinson's disease mimic: multiple system atrophy
metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: MSA masquerading as PD in a 74-year-old man with a prior essential tremor label, a family history of ET, vascular risk factors with small-vessel change and an old cerebellar lacune on MRI, and antihypertensives, tamsulosin and propranolol that could partly explain his orthostatic symptoms. The diagnosis requires integrating symmetric parkinsonism without rest tremor, a poor response to 600 mg/day levodopa, a cerebellar syndrome, neurogenic orthostatic hypotension with urge incontinence, nocturnal stridor and the MRI markers.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: The vascular and drug explanations for the ataxia and the orthostatic hypotension invite a wrong attribution; 1 required criterion (MRI) and 1 recommended (medication review)
metadata.revision_reason: October 2026 review round: plans/PD.md. Literature step deleted; medication review rewritten with the patient's own drugs; levodopa dose and medication list corrected (two tablets of 25/100 three times daily, 600 mg/day); seed remnants (jaw and joint pain, low-grade fever, rapid weight loss) removed; cerebellar signs and nocturnal stridor made explicit in the patient block; MRI gadolinium line and pontine area corrected; MIBG impression binary; DaTscan waste with a stored symmetric report; orthostatic, autonomic and tilt reports stored; clinically established MSA (MDS 2022); musts, differential, evidence and red herrings rewritten
metadata.seed_case_elements_used: Adapted from a source case of a 76-year-old man with hypertension, coronary disease, peripheral arterial disease, essential tremor and orthostatic symptoms. The clinical picture was transformed into a neurodegenerative parkinsonian syndrome; the source case's inflammatory features (jaw and joint pain, low-grade fever, raised ESR, IgA gammopathy) were removed in October 2026.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Heinrich Mayer is a 74-year-old right-handed retired mechanical engineer referred to the neurology movement disorders clinic for evaluation of progressive motor decline over the past sixteen months. He is accompanied by his wife, who provides substantial collateral history. The patient was originally diagnosed with essential tremor eight years ago by his primary care physician after presenting with bilateral hand tremor that was worse with action and partially responsive to propranolol. Over the past sixteen months, his wife has observed a gradual but relentless decline in his motor function that she considers qualitatively different from his long-standing tremor. He has become progressively slower in all activities of daily living: he takes twice as long to dress, needs assistance with buttons, and struggles with utensils during meals. His handwriting has become progressively smaller and illegible. His facial expression has diminished to the point that family members have asked whether he is depressed. Approximately ten months ago, he began experiencing episodes of lightheadedness and near-syncope upon standing, initially attributed to his antihypertensive medication. Amlodipine was reduced from 10 mg to 5 mg, then increased back to 10 mg when blood pressure remained elevated while supine, yet orthostatic symptoms persisted. He has had four near-falls and one complete fall while turning in the bathroom approximately three months ago, striking his shoulder. His wife reports that his balance difficulties seemed to appear relatively early in the course, within the first six months of symptom onset. Constipation has worsened despite daily polyethylene glycol, and he reports new urinary urgency with two episodes of urge incontinence in the past two months. He has lost about 3 kg over the past year, attributing this to fatigue and reduced appetite. His wife notes that his snoring has worsened dramatically over the past year, and for the past few months she has also heard a harsh, high-pitched noise when he breathes in during sleep, different from his old snoring. She has witnessed episodes where he appears to act out his dreams, on one occasion striking her while asleep. He also describes general muscular fatigue and proximal weakness, particularly when climbing stairs or rising from chairs, though he is unsure whether this represents true weakness or slowness. Notably, the tremor that was his original presenting symptom eight years ago appears to have changed in character or largely resolved; his wife reports that his hands no longer shake the way they used to. His primary care physician initiated a trial of carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg three times daily (300 mg/day levodopa) four months ago. After eight weeks with equivocal benefit (his wife estimates at most ten to fifteen percent subjective improvement in morning stiffness), the dose was increased to two tablets of 25/100 mg three times daily (600 mg/day levodopa), which he has now taken for six weeks with no further benefit.

neurological_exam.additional: Orthostatic vital signs: BP supine 148/90 mmHg, HR 68; BP standing at 1 minute 114/70 mmHg, HR 74; BP standing at 3 minutes 104/62 mmHg, HR 76. Patient reported lightheadedness and graying of vision on standing. Previous essential tremor diagnosis is questioned: the original tremor was reportedly bilateral postural and action tremor of the hands that responded partially to propranolol, but the current examination shows no clear action or postural tremor, only an intermittent, low-amplitude, irregular postural tremor. Mild anterocollis noted. No myoclonus. No dystonia.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing without dysmetria bilaterally. Heel-to-shin mildly ataxic bilaterally, with side-to-side deviation beyond what the slowness explains. Rapid alternating movements moderately slowed bilaterally.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, reactive to light. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus; horizontal smooth pursuit mildly saccadic. No vertical gaze palsy; vertical saccades of normal speed. Facial expression markedly hypomimic bilaterally. Mild bilateral jaw jerk. Hearing grossly intact. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline without fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Mildly wide-based gait with markedly reduced bilateral arm swing. Moderate postural instability on pull test: took 4 retropulsive steps on first attempt and required assistance on second attempt. Turning requires 6-7 steps with en bloc turning. No freezing of gait. Tandem walk not possible beyond 3 steps, with lateral deviation. Romberg mildly positive.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, date, and situation. MMSE 27/30, losing points on serial sevens (2 errors) and recall (missed 1 of 3 words, retrieved with category cue). MoCA 24/30, losing points on the trail-making item (1), serial subtraction (1), letter fluency (9 F-words in 60 seconds, 1) and delayed recall (2/5 words, retrieved 1 with cue, 3). Speech mildly hypophonic, with slurred and slightly irregular articulation. No aphasia.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk mildly reduced globally. Tone increased bilaterally with lead-pipe rigidity at wrists, elbows, and neck; cogwheel phenomenon difficult to elicit due to absence of concurrent tremor. Bradykinesia present bilaterally on finger tapping and hand opening/closing with early decrement and fatigue, approximately symmetric. No rest tremor and no sustained action tremor during a 10-minute examination; only an intermittent, low-amplitude, irregular postural tremor of the right hand, approximately 5-6 Hz, present from the onset of the posture. Strength 5/5 in all major muscle groups. No pronator drift.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric in biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar bilaterally. Achilles reflexes 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Babinski sign. Palmomental reflex present bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch and pinprick intact throughout. Vibration mildly reduced at great toes bilaterally. Proprioception intact. No cortical sensory loss.
